label: Complex Numbers: A Primer
notes: This chapter spans printed pages 297 through 310 and builds a geometric working model of complex numbers. We treat the field C not as an abstraction but as the plane equipped with rotation and scaling, the setting that will later let projective geometry encode Euclidean angle and distance uniformly.

label: Historical Pressure
notes: Complex numbers entered mathematics through polynomial solving, not through a wish for a new plane. The cubic formula for x cubed minus fifteen x minus four passes through non-real intermediate quantities even though every root is real. We want a field where roots can be counted without changing rules midstream.

label: The Complex Plane
notes: We identify the number a plus i b with the point of coordinates a and b, the Argand plane. Real and imaginary parts are Cartesian coordinates, while modulus and argument are polar coordinates. Addition is plain vector addition, a translation of the plane, which is the easy half of the arithmetic.

label: Polar Form and Multiplication
notes: Multiplication is the structured operation. Writing each number in polar form, the product multiplies the two moduli and adds the two arguments. Multiplication by a fixed w is therefore a similarity, a rotation by its argument composed with a scaling by its modulus, captured by a real two by two matrix.

label: Multiplication as Rotation-Scaling
notes: Here is the central picture. Point z sits at radius r and angle theta, point w at radius s and angle phi. Their product lands at radius r times s and angle theta plus phi. Trace the arguments adding on the diagram so students see rotation and scaling acting together as one similarity.

label: Conjugation as Reflection
notes: Conjugation sends a plus i b to a minus i b, a reflection in the real axis. It preserves both addition and multiplication, so it is a field automorphism of C. For real-coefficient polynomials this forces non-real roots to arrive in conjugate pairs, a rule we use repeatedly when reading factorizations.

label: Roots of Unity
notes: The n-th roots of unity solve z to the n equals one. Their common modulus is one and their arguments are equally spaced multiples of two pi over n, so they sit as vertices of a regular n-gon on the unit circle. Solving a power equation is angle division plus a branch choice.

label: Euler's Formula
notes: Euler's formula says e to the i theta equals cosine theta plus i sine theta, a point on the unit circle at angle theta. It makes multiplication's angle addition obvious through the exponential law, and it explains why argument is periodic: theta and theta plus two pi name the same point.

label: Fundamental Theorem of Algebra
notes: Over C every degree n polynomial factors completely into n linear factors, counting multiplicity. The field is algebraically closed. Conjugate symmetry organizes the real-coefficient case, and this closure is exactly the bookkeeping that makes intersection counting in projective geometry uniform and predictable.

label: Uniform Intersection Counting
notes: Take the unit circle and a vertical line. At x equals 0.65 the line cuts two real points; at x equals 1.35 it misses the real picture, yet the equation still has two complex solutions for y. Complex closure records the hidden intersection, so a line and a conic always meet twice with multiplicity.

label: Bridge to Projective Measurement
notes: Two consequences carry forward. First, complexifying coordinates lets projective constructions count intersections uniformly, the habit behind conics and the circular points at infinity. Second, conjugation is an automorphism, so the fundamental theorem of projective geometry gains a semilinear branch combining a matrix with conjugation over C.

label: Recap and Outlook
notes: Recap the geometric dictionary: points carry length and angle, multiplication is a similarity, roots form regular polygons, Euler ties angle to the exponential, and conjugation is reflection and automorphism. Algebraic closure is a measurement tool. Next we introduce complex points and the circular points to encode Euclidean angle and distance.
